title: CRISPR gene therapy for sickle cell disease
query: CRISPR gene therapy sickle cell disease
markdown:
## In plain English
Clinical research using CRISPR-based editing of patients' own blood‑forming (hematopoietic) stem cells shows promising results for sickle cell disease (SCD): several trials report large increases in fetal hemoglobin and a marked reduction or elimination of painful vaso‑occlusive crises after a single treatment. Most clinical work has targeted the erythroid enhancer of BCL11A to reactivate fetal hemoglobin. However, longer follow-up, larger numbers, and attention to delivery, durability, and safety remain important areas of ongoing study [PMID 33283989](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33283989/) [PMID 38661449](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38661449/) [PMID 42400217](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42400217/) [PMID 39794549](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39794549/).

## Key findings
- CRISPR-Cas9 editing of the erythroid-specific BCL11A enhancer in autologous CD34+ hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells increased fetal hemoglobin and produced transfusion independence in trial patients, with elimination of vaso‑occlusive events reported in an early SCD patient case [PMID 33283989](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33283989/).
- A phase 3 trial of exagamglogene autotemcel (exa‑cel), which edits the BCL11A enhancer ex vivo, showed that among patients evaluable at 12 months, 97% were free of severe vaso‑occlusive crises and 100% were free of hospitalizations for such crises; engraftment occurred in all treated patients and the safety profile reflected expected effects of myeloablative conditioning and autologous transplantation [PMID 38661449](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38661449/).
- Systematic reviews of clinical trials conclude that CRISPR/Cas9 disruption of BCL11A or γ‑globin promoters can strongly activate fetal hemoglobin and reduce clinical complications in thalassemia and SCD, and suggest CRISPR approaches as potential one‑time curative therapies in these inherited hemoglobin disorders [PMID 39794549](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39794549/) [PMID 42400217](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42400217/).
- Broader systematic syntheses of autologous gene‑therapy programs (including lentiviral, shmiR‑BCL11A, CRISPR‑Cas9, CRISPR‑Cas12a, and base editing) find high rates of clinical benefit (e.g., freedom from vaso‑occlusive events and transfusion independence) across different platforms in early follow‑up, but emphasize heterogeneity in endpoints and the need to evaluate feasibility of manufacturing, conditioning, and long‑term monitoring [PMID 42400217](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42400217/).
- Preclinical meta-analysis of animal studies found that CRISPR‑edited hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells engraft early similarly to controls but show reduced persistence at later time points and in secondary transplants, highlighting a potential durability challenge from preclinical data [PMID 33666363](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33666363/).

## How strong is the evidence?
The evidence includes randomized‑trial‑level and single‑group phase 3 interventional clinical data and multiple clinical trial reports summarized in recent systematic reviews. The phase 3 exa‑cel trial reported on 44 treated patients with median follow‑up ~19 months and formally prespecified clinical endpoints [PMID 38661449](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38661449/). Systematic reviews pooled results from dozens to over a hundred treated patients across programs (e.g., 115 patients in one review and 148 infused across programs in another) but noted heterogeneity in endpoints and follow‑up durations [PMID 39794549](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39794549/) [PMID 42400217](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42400217/). Preclinical animal meta‑analysis raises concerns about long‑term persistence of edited stem cells, indicating some remaining uncertainty about durability beyond available clinical follow‑up [PMID 33666363](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33666363/).

## Limitations and caveats
- These abstracts summarize early to mid‑term clinical follow‑up; long‑term durability (many years) and late safety outcomes are not fully established in the presented reports [PMID 38661449](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38661449/) [PMID 42400217](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42400217/).
- Preclinical animal studies suggest reduced persistence of edited stem cells over time and in secondary transplants, which may not fully predict human outcomes but indicates a potential durability issue not yet resolved by clinical reports [PMID 33666363](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33666363/).
- The trials and reviews cover multiple platforms and variable endpoints; heterogeneity in trial design, definitions of outcomes, and follow‑up limits straightforward comparison and pooled effect estimates [PMID 42400217](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42400217/) [PMID 39794549](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39794549/).
- The abstracts do not provide detailed information on rare adverse events, long‑term risks (e.g., insertional mutagenesis or other malignancy risks), cost, real‑world accessibility, or fertility effects; those issues require longer‑term and broader post‑marketing surveillance [PMID 38661449](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38661449/) [PMID 42400217](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42400217/).
